overview: The atlas label Papuan neolithic farmers covers no single people, language, state, or uniform stage. Its first polygon joins ten components across New Guinea, New Britain, Timor, Flores, Sumba, Maluku, and Sulawesi. Archaeology instead shows different local histories. At Kuk, highland gardeners maintained and altered wetland cultivation; around Caution Bay, coastal communities worked shell, fished, gathered reef foods, made settlements, and later met Lapita-linked pottery traditions. Northern Moluccan and Timorese sequences combine local continuities with new ceramics, animals, or contacts in different ways. Sulawesi evidence likewise resists a tidy replacement story. Dates are calibrated ranges, and many celebrated developments began before 1500 BCE or continued after 323 BCE. Family organization, teaching, healing, and waste disposal rarely leave direct labels, so this card separates preserved traces from plausible but unproved behavior. The word Neolithic is useful only as a cautious archaeological shorthand, not a ladder that every community climbed together. The atlas removes one Sulawesi component by 500 BCE and drops the id at 323 BCE, but those software seams record neither conquest nor collapse. People, landscapes, skills, and exchange continued.

periods.title: 1500 to 1350 BCE: a broad atlas umbrella begins
periods.summary: The exact id first appears in the 1500 BCE snapshot as ten disconnected components. Archaeological syntheses warn that pottery, domesticated plants, animals, and language spread did not arrive everywhere as one package. The start date is therefore a map seam, not a synchronized founding by one population.

periods.title: 1350 to 1200 BCE: northern Moluccan sequences stay local
periods.summary: Excavations in Halmahera, Kayoa, Morotai, and Gebe reveal differing site histories. Red-slipped pottery, ground stone, food remains, and introduced animals must be tied to particular layers. The atlas joins these islands to New Guinea, but the evidence does not reveal a common government or single community.

periods.title: 1200 to 1050 BCE: pottery dates overlap imperfectly
periods.summary: Bayesian estimates place initial ceramics at different times across Sulawesi, Pulau Ay, and Flores, often with wide ranges. These estimates overlap this teaching interval without pinpointing one migration year. Pottery is durable evidence for making, using, and discarding vessels, not an ethnic name stamped onto every sherd.

periods.title: 1050 to 900 BCE: Caution Bay joins wider Lapita worlds
periods.summary: At Caution Bay, Lapita-associated deposits begin around 2900 calibrated years ago, after earlier coastal occupation. Pottery, shell, stone, food remains, and a burial document a local community participating in broader connections. The evidence supports contact and settlement change, not the erasure of everyone already living nearby.

periods.title: 900 to 750 BCE: coastal foodways keep changing
periods.summary: Caution Bay shell assemblages span pre-Lapita and Lapita phases. Researchers track changes in collection and settlement while recognizing preservation and sampling limits. Reef foods and fishing mattered locally, but an excavated midden cannot supply a universal menu for every coast, island, age group, or season.

periods.title: 750 to 600 BCE: Kuk channels mark local work
periods.summary: Late Phase 3 at Kuk closely predates calibrated ranges around 700 to 400 BCE. Straight channels lowered water tables and organized wetland cultivation, yet their precise crop plots and social ownership remain debated. These engineered traces show coordinated labor at one highland wetland, not an empire-wide irrigation ministry.

periods.title: 600 to 450 BCE: Pain Haka preserves unequal detail
periods.summary: Pain Haka on Flores contains adults and children buried in positions, with some infants placed in jars and some graves furnished with pottery. Its broad dates cross this interval and extend later. The cemetery reveals local mortuary choices, while differences among burials resist a single regional rule.

periods.title: 450 to 323 BCE: a map label ends, communities continue
periods.summary: The target keeps nine components in 400 BCE, then disappears at the 323 BCE endpoint. No reviewed archaeological source identifies a matching fall. A separate papuan label appears only later in the atlas. The ending is therefore continuity through an editorial handoff, with no invented conqueror or vanished population.

sections.title: Read the atlas shape as a warning

items.text: The index contains one exact record named Papuan neolithic farmers, dated circa 1500 to 323 BCE and typed as a culture. Coverage confirms five intervals and no finished card. Those database facts identify the missing record; they do not prove that ancient residents shared this English name.

At 1500, 1000, and 700 BCE the decoded target is the same ten-component MultiPolygon with 609 positions. Its bounds stretch from Sulawesi to eastern New Guinea and from near the equator to Sumba. Such disconnected geography cannot responsibly be narrated as one fenced territory or capital.

The early shape includes tested points near Kuk, Tari, Goroka, Kainantu, Lae, lower Sepik, Fakfak, Wamena, Timika, Merauke, Kerema, Kupang, Flores, and Sumba. It excludes Wewak, Madang, Milne Bay, Manus, New Ireland, Bougainville, Waigeo, and Torres Strait from its mapped reach.

Between the 700 and 500 BCE snapshots, the atlas removes a 147-position Sulawesi component. The remaining nine components keep an identical later geometry through 400 BCE. That sharp edit is suspiciously cartographic: no cited excavation demonstrates a coordinated population withdrawal from the entire deleted outline.

The target shares no direct TopoJSON arc with another owner in any of its five snapshots. At a tested Sulawesi interior point, ownership changes to Austronesians in the 500 BCE file. That is an atlas classification switch, not proof that neighbors recognized a surveyed border or changed identity overnight.

sections.title: Build history from evidence, not stage labels

items.text: The Kuk monograph combines excavated features, sediments, plant evidence, and dating across a long highland sequence. Researchers revise interpretations when phases or contexts demand it. That method offers deep background for this card, never a template to force onto every later coast, cave, island, or community.

Pollen and charcoal records show forest disturbance and burning developed gradually in highland New Guinea, with different local histories. Such proxy evidence can reveal vegetation change and human activity over long spans. It cannot name individual gardeners, establish one ethnic frontier, or prove that every fire cleared a crop field.

Kuk excavations preserve an unusually long but incomplete wetland record. The monograph distinguishes changing phases instead of treating every ditch and mound as simultaneous. Its importance comes from that local sequence; it does not license filling blank regions, islands, or centuries with identical gardens and social arrangements.

At Tanamu 1, researchers distinguish pre-Lapita, Lapita, and post-Lapita deposits within a sequence longer than five thousand years. Those categories organize changing materials at one Caution Bay site. They should not become three universal chapters imposed on Timor, Sulawesi, the highlands, or every island in the polygon.

Sulawesi caves preserve a Toalean archaeological tradition before later pottery and ground axes. Researchers consider continuity, contact, diffusion, and disturbance rather than assuming a clean replacement. This matters because the atlas deletes Sulawesi at one seam: its polygon change cannot settle questions that excavated layers leave complex.

sections.title: Grow, gather, hunt and fish locally

items.text: Kuk plant evidence includes starches and phytoliths studied to identify taro, banana, and other plant use. Vegetative crops often preserve poorly, so researchers combine microscopic traces with features and chronology. A residue can support cultivation history, but it cannot recover a complete 700 BCE supper or every crop variety.

New Guinea plant research shows long histories of cultivating vegetatively propagated crops, including bananas, taro, and yams, while emphasizing how difficult those plants are to trace. Highland gardeners changed practices over time; they were not simply following one timeless recipe handed unchanged across every New Guinea community.

Timor cave plant remains do not show rice or millet arriving with the earliest pottery and introduced animals. That negative result challenges the familiar bundle of farmers, cereals, pots, and livestock moving together. People could adopt objects or animals selectively while maintaining locally rooted plant economies and choices.

Northern Moluccan faunal deposits contain fish, shell, phalanger, and, in suitable phases, pig or dog remains. Preservation and sample size vary by site and layer. These bones illuminate local meals and animal movement, but they cannot establish one diet for Halmahera, New Guinea, Flores, and Timor.

Caution Bay deposits show long use of near-shore shellfish before and during Lapita-associated settlement. Gathering required detailed knowledge of reefs, tides, seasons, and safe handling, although archaeology rarely records the words for that knowledge. The midden is a food archive, but thankfully not a restaurant menu with prices.

sections.title: Make tools, pots and managed landscapes

items.text: Phase 3 channels at Kuk were straight, deliberate cuts that helped lower the wetland water table. Their construction required observation, planning, tools, and repeated maintenance. Calling them drainage is justified; calling them sewers is not. Their excavated form records agricultural engineering, not the full organization of the workers.

Uattamdi residents selected stone and shell alongside making and using pottery in a stratified island sequence. These materials show practiced production and exchange without revealing a single inventor or palace workshop. Skill can endure, travel, and change through ordinary communities, even when the surviving object lacks its maker's name.

Uattamdi layers preserve pottery, stone artifacts, and changing occupation beginning around the late second millennium BCE. Forms and surfaces belong to a site sequence, not a universal Moluccan style. Stratigraphy lets archaeologists order deposits, while radiocarbon ranges keep the story appropriately fuzzier than a royal year list.

Northern Moluccan pottery specialists varied clay fabrics, vessel forms, surfaces, red slip, and decoration through time and place. Those decisions record technical knowledge and social preferences. A pot can travel beyond its maker, so decoration alone should not be treated as a passport proving the language or ancestry of its user.

At Caution Bay, shell working predates Lapita ceramics and links local makers to a wider circum-New Guinea arena. Cutting and shaping shell demanded practiced choices about raw material and form. That achievement belongs to specific communities; later pottery does not turn earlier artisans into passive people awaiting outside technology.

sections.title: Travel and exchange without inventing one migration

items.text: Initial pottery estimates differ markedly: Sulawesi, Pulau Ay, and Flores each have broad, partly overlapping modeled ranges. The pattern supports multiple routes and tempos rather than a single fleet arriving everywhere in one year. Bayesian chronology improves comparison, but its probability ranges must remain visible in a child-friendly story.

Asitau Kuru on Timor preserves occupation across tens of thousands of years, with a locally defined Neolithic phase beginning around 3800 years ago. That cave sequence combines continuity and change. It offers no warrant for calling all residents of Timor members of a new, uniform farming nation.

Caution Bay Lapita deposits connect the south coast of New Guinea to a broad pottery-making and voyaging world around 2900 calibrated years ago. Earlier occupation remained part of the local sequence. Connections could move vessels, styles, foods, people, and ideas in different combinations rather than replacing every household.

Moiapu 3 preserves terminal Lapita ceramics and a local settlement history near the end of that named tradition. Pig and dog evidence is scarce or uncertain, which warns against checking off a standard migration package. People adopted, rejected, or reworked materials within particular coastal relationships.

The broad atlas outline spans sea passages among many islands, yet no vessel survives merely because a polygon connects shores. Obsidian, shell, pottery, and introduced animals instead provide indirect evidence of movement. Archaeologists compare sources and contexts; the map alone cannot tell who sailed, why, or in whose canoe.

sections.title: Keep households and social life plural

items.text: Caution Bay settlements, food remains, working debris, and burials show people living together and returning to places over time. These traces support households and communities in a broad sense. They do not securely reveal whether residence was matrilocal, patrilocal, flexible, or organized by categories used by any modern group.

Pain Haka graves differ in body position, orientation, containers, and pottery. Variation can reflect age, identity, sequence, circumstance, or choices now lost. The cemetery demonstrates social attention to the dead, but its excavators cannot turn every difference into a fixed rank or island-wide family rule.

At Kuk, maintaining channels and cultivation surfaces required coordinated labor across repeated seasons. Archaeology records cuts, fills, and plant traces more readily than conversation or kinship. Families may have participated, but the preserved features do not identify a chief, workforce size, inheritance rule, or who made the snack breaks happen.

Uattamdi occupation debris combines vessels, stone, shell, and food remains in layered contexts. Repeated deposition implies shared routines and social spaces, yet a cave or rockshelter is not automatically a permanent village house. Household composition and sleeping arrangements remain unknown unless the deposits supply stronger architectural evidence.

The atlas label joins highlands, coasts, large islands, and small islands where social arrangements need not match. Archaeological comparison is most useful when it preserves those differences. One shared card can introduce evidence, but it must not manufacture a timeless Papuan family system across eleven centuries and thousands of kilometers.

sections.title: Let children learn through participation, cautiously

items.text: Pain Haka includes children and infants, some placed in pottery jars. Their presence proves that age mattered in local mortuary decisions and that children belonged within remembered community life. It does not reveal their names, games, daily chores, or whether every child received the same treatment.

Shell shaping, pottery forming, gardening, fishing, and reef collecting all require learned sequences of action. Archaeological products show accomplished practice, but usually not the lesson itself. Children may have learned by watching and helping; that remains a careful inference, not evidence for formal schools or uniform ages.

Pottery variation in the northern Moluccas records choices repeated by makers over time. Such patterned craft implies knowledge transmission, correction, and memory. The vessels do not identify whether teachers were parents, other relatives, specialists, peers, or several of these, so the card avoids assigning a classroom to the past.

Planting vegetatively propagated crops involves selecting pieces, preparing ground, timing work, and recognizing healthy growth. New Guinea plant archaeology shows the antiquity of these practices while rarely identifying learners. Young people likely encountered this knowledge, but no excavated ditch comes with a tidy ancient homework sheet.

A dog from terminal Lapita Edubu was directly dated and genetically studied, giving rare evidence for an animal living near people. It says nothing secure about pets, children feeding puppies, hunting lessons, or names. Those delightful possibilities belong in imagination unless stronger contextual evidence appears.

sections.title: Discuss health, care and death without inventing medicine

items.text: Pain Haka human remains permit study of age, burial practice, and some bodily evidence, but the cemetery report does not provide a medical handbook. Care for the dead is visible; diagnosis and treatment in life are much harder. The card therefore avoids naming healers, remedies, or diseases without exact supporting traces.

Northern Moluccan human-remains studies include samples assigned to different phases, many later than this card or too broad for a clean 1500 to 323 BCE claim. Their health findings cannot simply be pasted backward. Chronological mismatch is evidence discipline, not a boring footnote trying to ruin the story.

Kuk plant residues and microscopic traces support processing and cultivation, but they do not securely distinguish food, medicine, cordage, or another use for every fragment. Modern medicinal knowledge must not be projected backward. Archaeology can identify a substance while leaving its exact purpose honestly unresolved.

Caution Bay shell, fish, and other food remains help reconstruct diet and resource use. Diet matters to health, yet a midden cannot diagnose a particular person's deficiency, fever, injury, or care. Population-wide claims require skeletal and contextual evidence dated to the same place and period.

Kuk's managed wetland changed water and working conditions, but excavated channels do not reveal whether residents boiled drinking water, treated wounds, assisted births, or isolated illness. Some form of care surely existed in human communities; its precise practices remain undocumented here, so no remedy is invented.

sections.title: Follow water, refuse and the missing toilets

items.text: Kuk channels managed agricultural wetness by moving or lowering water around cultivated surfaces. They are strong evidence for landscape engineering and maintenance. They are not identified as drinking-water pipes, storm drains for houses, or sewers. One ditch can be impressive without volunteering for every modern plumbing job.

Wetland preservation at Kuk records buried cuts, fills, and plant traces unevenly. Waterlogged conditions can protect some organic evidence while destroying or confusing other signals. Archaeologists reconstruct sequences from sediments and relationships, not from a perfectly preserved farm plan labeled kitchen, bathroom, and compost heap.

At coastal sites, shells and bones accumulated in deposits that help identify food use and discard. Concentrated refuse shows where some material ended up, but does not automatically reveal formal rubbish rules. Cleaning, sweeping, reuse, burning, tidal removal, and decay may leave very different archaeological signatures.

No securely published latrine or toilet has been identified for this exact atlas umbrella and interval in the reviewed sources. That absence does not mean people ignored privacy or cleanliness; it means organic waste rarely survives with a helpful sign. The card declines to turn silence into a universal habit.

Caution Bay middens record repeated disposal near lived places, while Kuk drainage records purposeful water control. Together they show practical management of surroundings in different settings. Neither supports a single regional sanitation system, and neither tells us how every household handled drinking water, bathing, washing, or human waste.

sections.title: Preserve silence about writing and the ending

items.text: Written-language sample: none securely attributable to these communities between 1500 and 323 BCE. The reviewed archaeological sources provide objects, sediments, food remains, and human burials, not a deciphered local inscription. Repeated pottery designs may communicate identity or memory, but they are not safely transcribed as words.

Motu received a developed orthography and school publication in 1877, more than two thousand years after this card ends. Printing a later Motu phrase here would falsely assign one language and spelling system to diverse ancient communities. The honest sample is therefore absence, with the later date explaining why.

The broad word Papuan groups many non-Austronesian languages by contrast, not one ancestral language recoverable from this polygon. Archaeological layers do not automatically disclose speech. This card avoids attaching modern ethnonyms or present-day language names to people at Kuk, Pain Haka, Uattamdi, or Caution Bay.

At 323 BCE the atlas id vanishes, but none of the cited sites records a matching destruction horizon across the mapped components. Cultivation, exchange, craft, settlement, and family life continued through locally different histories. The ending field is continuity, with no fall date and no invented successor state.

The strongest achievement is not a single monument. It is sustained expertise: gardeners reshaping wet ground, coastal families reading reefs, artisans mastering stone, shell, and clay, and travelers maintaining island connections. Those achievements become clearer when the atlas umbrella is opened into many local stories instead of one imaginary civilization.

ending.text: The 323 BCE endpoint is the atlas record's last software boundary, not a documented conquest, migration, or collapse. The nine remaining components disappear under this id, while later atlas labels use different names and shapes. Local communities, cultivation, travel, craft, languages, family life, and changing settlements continued beyond the card's editorial window.
